title: Effects of menstrual cycle phases on athletic performance and related physiological outcomes: a systematic review of studies using high methodological standards
authors: Schlie J, Krassowski V, Schmidt A
population: Eumenorrheic females in studies that measured 17-beta-estradiol, progesterone and LH, with performance tested in 2 or more phases
findings: Only 19 studies (total n = 279, 25.6 +/- 3.6 y, mean n = 13.9 +/- 7) met the hormone-verification standard; elite athletes were underrepresented and serum hormone analysis in elite sport appeared poor.
58% of included studies reported a significant phase effect on at least one performance-related outcome, but direction and magnitude varied between studies.

Early follicular phase was unfavourable for VO2max in one study and peak power in two studies; submaximal ventilation was reduced in the early follicular phase; maximum and explosive strength were largely unaffected; neuromuscular coordination improved at ovulation.
Medium to high risk of bias in randomisation and reported outcomes; authors advise critical interpretation of conclusions about presence or absence of cycle effects.
limitations: Very small studies and heterogeneous phases and populations prevented quantitative synthesis; most findings come from single studies. Supports uncertainty rather than a rule.
implications: Confirms McNulty with a hormone-verified sample: keep cycle phase out of automatic load prescription.
Treat self-reported phase (calendar counting, app-based) as low-validity input and label phase estimates as approximate.
Frame any cycle feature as an optional awareness and symptom-tracking tool, not a performance predictor.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (J Appl Physiol, 2025-09). Europe PMC abstract (PMID 40695607) supports all numbers. Evidence level lowered from A to B because the review itself reports medium/high bias and no quantitative synthesis.
